title: As hard to hold as the wind
hookLine: Arjuna tells Krishna the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Vyasa maps its five grounds
carry: abhyasa and vairagya hold the restless mind
tomorrow: What did Ratnakara ask his family?

lines: AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.
cards: On the battlefield in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna has just described the yogi whose mind is steady, the same toward friend and enemy. And Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, pushes back.
Krishna, he says, the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. Krishna doesn't argue.
Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held, by practice, and by letting go.

teach.b: Patanjali names the same pair in the Yoga Sutra: the mind's movements are stilled by abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go.

And the first commentary on the Sutra is credited by tradition to Vyasa, the name tradition also gives the sage behind the Mahabharata. In his very first comment, he does something Arjuna would appreciate.

teach.h: VYASA: FIVE GROUNDS OF THE MIND.
teach.b: Yoga, he says, is samadhi, the settled, absorbed mind, and the mind has five grounds. Kshipta, scattered, thrown in every direction. Mudha, dull, heavy and fogged over.
Vikshipta, distracted, settling now and then but pulled away again. Ekagra, one-pointed, resting on a single thing. And niruddha, stilled, the turnings quieted.
Vyasa is strict: the steady moments of a distracted mind don't count as yoga yet, because the distraction swallows them.
Yoga proper belongs to the one-pointed and the stilled.

teach.h: A WEATHER REPORT, NOT A GRADE.
teach.b: But read the list as a weather report, not a grade. It describes skies, not kinds of people, and one person can pass under several before lunch. That's the teaching to carry.

Hindu yoga doesn't scold the restless mind; even Arjuna had one. It asks which ground you're on, then hands you the Gita's two tools: come back, again and again, and loosen your grip on what pulls you away.

how: Students of Yoga philosophy read the Yoga Sutras with Vyasa's commentary, often alongside Krishna's answer to Arjuna in the Gita, and teachers use the five grounds of the mind to help a student see where their attention is before they practice.

o: a breathing drill done before morning prayers
a set of poses that keep the body loose and strong
in Vyasa's reading, samadhi: a settled, absorbed mind

games.q: Vyasa's grounds of the mind — tap the pairs.
p: practice: coming back again and again
letting go of what pulls you

s: in the Gita, Krishna agrees with Arjuna that the mind is hard to hold
then he names the way: practice, and letting go.
for Vyasa, the steady moments of a distracted mind already count as yoga
he says the distraction swallows them; yoga proper is the one-pointed and the stilled.
the five grounds sort people into good and bad
they describe states of the mind, and one person can pass through several in a day.

games.q: you sit down to practice, and the mind is foggy and heavy, like it hasn't woken up. in Vyasa's list, which ground is this?
games.why: mudha. Vyasa names it without blame, the way a forecaster names fog. knowing the sky is where the practice starts.

practice: First, just check: is the mind racing, heavy, or coming and going? Name it once, without arguing. Then rest on one thing, the feel of your hands in your lap.
When attention drifts, that's the wind; notice it, let go of whatever pulled you, and come back. That coming back is abhyasa. If you pray, you can rest on a name you pray with instead.

wordCard.voice: Yoga. In Vyasa's first comment, yoga is samadhi, and the mind has five grounds: scattered, dull, distracted, one-pointed and stilled.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ground or level; the word used for the five grounds of the mind in Vyasa's commentary.

carryVoice: Your line: abhyasa and vairagya hold the restless mind. Even Arjuna's mind blew like wind. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.33–35 (Arjuna: the mind is restless and as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna: by practice and detachment it is held)
Yoga Sutras 1.12 (the movements of the mind are stilled by practice and non-attachment)
Yoga Sutras 1.1 (now, the teaching of yoga)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.1 (yoga is samadhi; the five grounds: kshipta, mudha, vikshipta, ekagra, niruddha; distracted samadhi is not yoga)
